titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Paraguay

div.head: 408. Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Paraguay
div.p: 41359. Subject: DAS Gelbard’s Conversation with Paraguayan Foreign Minister Saldivar.

2. As mentioned reftel, Paraguayan Foreign Minister Saldivar telephoned ARA DAS Gelbard on February 10 just as Paraguayan Ambassador Martinez had entered Gelbard’s office to receive the USG’s formal protest against the teargassing of Ambassador Taylor. Saldivar was clearly uncomfortable; he began with a lengthy, highly apologetic monologue, which gave the impression that the police officials who caused the incident had not been acting on the basis of instructions from higher authority. Saldivar repeatedly expressed his deep regrets for this incident. He noted his complete awareness of Gelbard’s previous conversations with Ambassador Martinez in the wake of Minister of Interior Montanaro’s statements against Ambassador Taylor. In this regard, he stated that he had provided the guarantees of security for Ambassador Taylor and all Americans in Paraguay pursuant to Gelbard’s request.

3. Gelbard responded by covering essentially the same points as in his conversation with Ambassador Martinez (reftel). He expressed extreme concern about the direction in which the GOP was taking bilateral relations. If the police were not acting from higher level instructions, he asked rhetorically, does this mean that the Paraguayan Government’s control is breaking down? The USG has responsibility for the safety of its citizens and
we had to wonder if we should alert American citizens to possible dangers which could befall them in Paraguay. Should we ask the American Davis Cup team to postpone or cancel the matches set for Asuncion in March? It was clear, at any rate, that the earlier statement of security guarantees given privately had had no worth. It was also clear that this incident represented a serious violation of the Vienna Convention, since the police were fully cognizant of the presence of Ambassador Taylor at the dinner and were in violation of some of the basic concepts of international conduct. Gelbard noted that in his visit to Asuncion last July GOP officials had spoken throughout of Paraguay’s vaunted “peace and tranquility;” it was clear that this does not exist and it was clear that the GOP was trying to make Ambassador Taylor a scapegoat for the complete range of Paraguay’s economic, political and social problems. Gelbard said that it was imperative, at this point, in order to allay USG concerns for the GOP to make a public apology to Ambassador Taylor and to the Paraguayans present at the dinner and to repeat publicly the guarantees of security for Ambassador Taylor and all Americans in Paraguay. Gelbard concluded by saying that the USG wants good relations with Paraguay. Our Ambassador was acting in ways that were fully consonant with accepted international behavior, contrary to the GOP’s statements. At this point, we needed clear signs from the GOP that it wants good bilateral relations with US.

4. Saldivar pleaded for USG assistance in helping the GOP find a way out of this problem. He urged that we not “humiliate” them. Gelbard said that we certainly did not wish to do that and under the circumstances the public statement was a minimal request. Gelbard also noted that we, of course, expect the GOP and their associates in the Colorado Party to live up completely to the accepted standards of international behavior.
4. Saldivar closed by saying that he had spoken with Ambassador Taylor several times already and expected to work with him closely to resolve this extremely unfortunate incident.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D870110–0254. Confidential; Immediate. Sent for information to Buenos Aires, Brasilia, and Montevideo. Drafted and approved by Gelbard.

In telegram 555 from Asuncion, February 10, the Embassy wrote: “Ambassador and Mrs. Taylor and other diplomats were tear gassed in Asuncion on February 9, while attending a reception at a private residence in the Ambassador’s honor hosted by a nonpartisan group called Mujeres por la Democracia (Women for Democracy) a group equivalent to our League of Women voters. The event occurred when the police threw up a cordon around the neighborhood to prevent invitees from attending the reception. After consulting with higher authorities, the police permitted diplomats to enter, after carefully checking their credentials. Then, after the well-heeled and smartly-dressed invitees plus onlookers being held on the periphery, whose number had grown to three hundred or more, did not disperse, the police called in their equivalent of a SWAT team and began launching tear gas at this group. Then, about a half-hour later, clearly aware of the presence of the Ambassador, his wife, and other U.S. and Argentine diplomats, who had previously identified themselves to the police and had been allowed to pass into the residence, the police launched a tear gas grenade from the adjoining property onto the rear patio where the diplomats, and those few Paraguayans who arrived before the police, were assembled.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D870445–0034)

In telegram 22319 to Asuncion, January 27, the Department wrote that Gelbard had “urgently summoned Paraguayan Ambassador Martínez to the Department on January 23 to express the Department’s deep concern over the threatening tone of the recent spate of public attacks on Ambassador Taylor spear-headed by Interior Minister Montanaro.” Gelbard stressed that “the USG will hold Montanaro, and the GOP, responsible should any harm befall Ambassador Taylor, or any member of the American community resident in Paraguay.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D870065–0169)

Gelbard visited Paraguay July 19–23, 1986 and met with Stroessner on July 22. (Telegram 2766 from Asuncion, July 24, 1986; Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D860568–0300) In telegram 2795 from Asuncion, July 25, 1986, the Embassy wrote: “Gelbard’s visit to Paraguay was busy and advanced U.S. objectives. Government contacts have apparently made up their minds in advance to view the visit in a favorable light and did not take umbrage at clear statements of the need for the GOP to begin a process of political opening. Opposition contacts were uniformly pleased with the private and public message they heard about the U.S. commitment to convincing the GOP to open the political process. Gelbard’s call for pragmatism was universally accepted. Press coverage was extensive, and most of the message delivered in private conversation also found its way in to the public domain even before the departure press conference. We expect to see no dramatic change in the mind-set of the GOP, but believe the visit will encourage the moderate forces in the Colorado party and the political opposition to echo his message with their own preoccupations over the future direction of the country.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D860572–0551)
